title: Data centres asymmetrically exacerbate energy burdens through wholesale price increases and regressive grid cost shifting - Nature Energy
text:
AbstractRapid artificial intelligence growth is driving energy-intensive data centre expansion, but its consequences for energy burdens and household welfare remain understudied. Here we show how data centre expansion asymmetrically deepens energy burdens across the USA through different channels, using causal analysis of price records, together with transmission plans and regulatory cost-allocation dockets. In wholesale markets, cumulative price increases attributable to data centres exceed 10% in the most exposed hubs by 2025. In regulated tariffs, residential users are allocated a median of 47% of costs despite contributing far less to demand growth. These channels produce compounding asymmetric energy burdens. Spatially, cost sharing forces rural communities to bear burden increases 76% larger than urban communities. Economically, the lowest-income households face extra energy burdens up to 28 percentage points. Fiscally, local economic returns are almost unrelated to spending, with a spending elasticity of 0.16. The states absorbing the largest energy burden increases capture the smallest returns.

Data availability

The minimum dataset supporting the findings of this study, including aggregated state-, city- and load-zone-level data centre capacity, publicly redistributable input and processed data and the regulatory docket records used in the cost-allocation analysis, is publicly available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23019736 (ref. 92). The facility-level data centre inventory used in this study was obtained from S&P Capital IQ Pro and 451 Research under a commercial licence and cannot be redistributed by the authors. These proprietary data may be obtained directly from S&P Global subject to its licensing terms. Source data are provided with this paper.
Code availability

All custom code used for data processing, statistical analysis and figure generation is publicly available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23019736 (ref. 92), including pinned software dependencies, installation instructions and scripts for reproducing the analyses and figures.
